To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the capabilities of learning from full positive data with a bounded number of subset queries and a bounded number (or even one) of equivalence queries (or subset queries) are incomparable, and that a bounded number of equivalence queries can be simulated by a bounded number of superset queries.

(a) subset and equivalence queries are incomparable in their learning power, (b) subset and subset queries with counterexamples are also incomparable in their power, (c) superset and subset queries are incomparable, but superset and subset with counterexamples are not, and (d) superset and equivalence queries are comparable in their power, and so are superset and equivalence with counterexamples, but superset with counterexamples is more powerful than equivalence queries with counterexamples

(a) a finite number of equivalence queries is sufficient to learn languages from positive data and a finite number of queries to an oracle; (b) a finite number (bounded by a computable function) of superset queries is sufficient to do the same; (c) a finite number subset queries is sufficient, if learners do not receive any counterexamples and may make unbounded number of mistakes.
In summary, our research is concerned with
learning from positive data and a finite number of queries.
the computational complexity of learning languages from full positive data, and with the capabilities of various types of queries.

the following question: how many queries are needed to simulate a given type of queries? We have found that, in many cases, a small number of subset queries can simulate an arbitrary number of queries of a different type.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the number of equivalence queries is more informative than the number of subset or superset queries.
, in most cases, a bounded number of equivalence queries with counterexamples is the best approach.
, in general, the number of queries of one type cannot be simulated by the number of queries in another type, but in some cases, the latter can be simulated by the former.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the number of equivalence queries is the most powerful, and the number of arbitrary counterexamples is the least powerful.
a bounded number of equivalence queries is the best type of queries for language learning, but a bounded number of subset queries may be a good alternative in certain situations.

a finite number of equivalence queries is more powerful than any finite number of other types of queries, except for subset queries when learners are behaviourally correct and may have unboundedly many errors.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the learning process can be significantly accelerated if a learner has access to a teacher.
a small number of queries can be very powerful and can be used for efficient language identification.
the number of queries and types of queries matter.
